Equity Release (Lifetime Mortgage) Calculator

If you're 55 or over and much of your wealth is sitting in your home, equity release is a way of turning some of it back into cash. One thing is worth saying before anything else, though. You don't make monthly payments, so the interest is added to the loan and then earns interest itself. Over the years, that can wear away the value you'd hoped to pass on.
blocks.2:
The Reality Check: How It Works

If you're a homeowner aged 55 or over, equity release lets you take some of your home's value as tax-free cash. The most common version is a loan secured on the home that's only repaid when you die or move into long-term care. That product is called a Lifetime Mortgage. The home stays yours throughout.

The Compound Interest Trap

With a normal mortgage you pay the interest off every month. Here it's added to the loan instead, so next month you're paying interest on the interest.

Example: Borrow £50k at 6%.
Year 1: You owe £53,000.
Year 15: You owe £120,000.
The debt grows faster each year than the year before, and it's the inheritance you'd planned to leave that absorbs the growth.

The "No Negative Equity" Guarantee

There's a safety net. Under Equity Release Council standards, you and your estate will never owe more than the property is worth.

Say the debt reaches £500k but the house sells for £400k. The lender writes off the £100k gap. Your family won't inherit a debt, though they might inherit £0.

Key Risks to Consider

  • Early Repayment Charges (ERCs): If you try to repay early in the first few years, some lenders charge up to 25% of the loan. It's a figure that only makes sense if you're sure the loan is for life.
  • Means Tested Benefits: Having £50,000 in the bank can cost you Council Tax Support or Pension Credit, so it's worth checking before you draw the money.
  • Moving Home: You can usually take the mortgage with you, which lenders call porting, but the new property has to meet their criteria. Retirement flats are often turned down.
